title: TA7-14884
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, (the principal claimant) and her son XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, both citizens of Saint Lucia, are seeking refugee protection pursuant to ss. 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
The principal claimant was appointed to act as designated representative on behalf of her minor son.

The claimant came to Canada because she was abused by her son's father. She sustained injuries and he threatened to kill her. As a result of the abuse, the principal claimant moved, however, she learned from her girlfriend that the perpetrator is still looking for her. As a result, she decided to come to Canada.
She arrived in Canada on December 19, 2006 and filed a refugee claim on December 13, 2007.
The Board finds that the claimant is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection.
The claimant has established her identity as per the certified true copy of her passport.1 CHAIRPERSON'S GUIDELINES

The Board has considered the gender guidelines2 before arriving at our decision. We accept that the claimant was abused during her relationship with the father of her child. Further, when they parted ways, he continued to threaten and harass her at her place of work.
The determinative issue is state protection.

The Board, in assessing the issue of state protection, is guided by a number of cases from the Federal Court and the Supreme Court of Canada. There is a presumption, except in situations where the state is in a complete breakdown, that it is capable of protecting its citizens. A claimant can rebut this presumption by providing clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect. The onus is on the claimant to approach the state for protection in situations where state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.3

No government is expected to guarantee perfect protection to all of its citizens at all times, and the fact that a state is not always successful in protecting its citizens is not enough to justify a claim, especially where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police, and civil authorities in place and is making serious efforts to protect its citizens.4 Less than perfect protection is not a basis to determine that the state is either unwilling or unable to offer reasonable protection.5
The Board must consider what steps the principal claimant took to seek state protection.

According to the claimant's narrative of her Personal Information Form (PIF), she sustained injury on two occasions, requiring medical attention. She acknowledged that two medical reports were made. Yet she was unable to provide any corroborative evidence. According to the principal claimant, she had asked her family to provide the reports, but they had been unable to access them. The principal claimant did not approach the police following either of these two incidents. She alleged that she was frightened, however, she also stated that her perpetrator followed her to the hospital which precluded her contacting the police. Nevertheless, she acknowledged she had not contacted the police after she left the hospital.

The only time the principal claimant approached the police was in 2002, following a threat at her mother's house, when she was roughed up by her perpetrator. She telephoned the police, following which she was advised that he was given a warning. The principal claimant believed that this was insufficient; she wanted him to be arrested. The principal claimant acknowledged that there is a police report regarding this incident, however again her family were unable to obtain a copy.

The principal claimant's PIF6 is virtually silent on what occurred following the incidents from 2000 until 2002. The only indication of ongoing problems was stated as follows: "he would come to my work but my boss would send him away"; this, in spite of an amended PIF submitted at the outset of the hearing. Nevertheless, the claimant acknowledged that at no time later did she report any ongoing harassment or threats as she did not believe that the police would arrest her ex-partner or provide assistance to her.

The Board concludes that the principal claimant was not diligent in pursuing state protection. The Board specifically notes the two incidents in which the principal claimant sustained injury and in which she made no reports to the police. Yet when roughed up later at her mother's house, she telephoned the police. At no time since 2002, did the claimant contact the police or any other state authority.

Documentary evidence indicates that Saint Lucia is a democracy, with a functioning and independent judiciary.7 The Royal Saint Lucia Police Force provides security and order. The police force is described as hierarchical, allowing for redress to a higher level if a complainant is dissatisfied with services. The Police Complaints Commission reviews cases of alleged police misconduct or ineffectiveness.8 In October 2007, officers from the United Kingdom were contracted to enhance police administrative and intelligence capacities. (ibid)

The Board would be remiss not to acknowledge that violence against women remains a problem, although independent sources suggest the government is responding to the problem. Nevertheless, it is noted that a non-governmental organization (CAFRA) does not view the efforts as being effective.9 Furthermore, counsel submits that police often do not take complaints seriously, however, it is also noted that victims often withdraw complaints. This, in counsel's opinion, corroborates why the principal claimant did not seek state protection. Counsel further argues that the information contained in the documentary evidence10 pre-dates the foregoing information and suggests that little change has occurred in the country during this time.

The Ministry of Health, Human Services and Gender Relations is responsible for addressing the problem of domestic violence. The increased recognition of gender-based violence has led to the government and advocacy groups being able to offer better protection to victims.11 The Domestic Violence Act (1995)12 prohibits violence against women and children and has provisions for Protection Orders and Occupation Orders, which can remove the abuser from the home. There is a special Family Court to deal with domestic violence issues and generally, the laws are enforced.13 The Court is described as victim friendly and an applicant does not require the services of a lawyer to proceed. Social workers at the Court assist victims in obtaining Protection Orders and conduct investigations of allegations to determine urgency of need.14 Police have undertaken special gender sensitivity training.15 Although it is acknowledged that some are still reticent to intervene, response speed is often attributed to a lack of police transportation.16

The documentary evidence also indicates that support services for physical, sexual and emotional abuse are available at the Saint Lucia Crisis Centre for Women. In addition, the Women's Support Centre, which is a government-supported shelter for women, provides residential services, crisis intervention, counselling, education out-reach, and assists victims with applications at court for Protection Orders.17 The Centre has a 24-hour hotline and can arrange to pick up victims at any time.18

Documentary evidence confirms that there are investigations, prosecutions and convictions and protection Orders issued in domestic assault situations. The statistics bear this out. Problems with reporting continue as victims are often reluctant to come forward and follow through with laying charges, or they withdraw due to financial dependency on the perpetrator.

The claimant does not believe that she would be afforded state protection as the police in her opinion do not take the necessary action. The Board finds that this statement is vague, speculative and inconsistent with what objective agencies who observe conditions in St. Lucia indicate. The Board finds, based on the documentary evidence before it, that there is an effective security force in place and that police reluctance, although existing, is not generalized.

Having given due consideration to the evidence before it, the Board finds that the principal claimant is not a Convention refugee and that, on a balance of probabilities, her removal to St. Lucia would not subject her personally to a risk to her life, a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture.

Accordingly, the principal claimant's claim is rejected. As well, her son's claim, which is based on her allegations, is also rejected.
